title: The 'Foamy' Brain Cells Linked to Aggressive MS
hook: Why does multiple sclerosis race ahead in some people and stay quiet in others? Brain tissue from severe cases reveals fat-stuffed immune cells that may flip from repair mode to relentless damage.
key_points: Why MS progresses quickly in some people and slowly in others has been unclear.
In brain tissue from severe MS cases, researchers found large numbers of 'foamy' immune cells packed with fat droplets.
The fat comes from myelin, the nerve coating that MS damages.
These overloaded cells appear to switch from helping repair the brain to fueling ongoing inflammation.
The finding points to a possible new target for slowing aggressive MS.
content_html: Multiple sclerosis can be unpredictable: some people's disease creeps along for decades, while others decline rapidly. Scientists have long wanted to know what separates the two — and a new discovery in brain tissue offers a clue.
extra_html:
As ScienceDaily reports, researchers examining brain tissue from patients with severe MS found large numbers of "foamy" immune cells stuffed with fat droplets — fat that comes from myelin, the protective coating around nerve fibers that MS progressively strips away. These immune cells normally help clean up damaged myelin as part of repair. But once overloaded with fat, they appear to switch roles, shifting from cleanup crew to a source of ongoing inflammation and damage.

The discovery doesn't change treatment today, but it suggests a promising target: if these overloaded cells can be identified or defused before they turn harmful, it could open a new way to slow the aggressive form of a disease that currently progresses differently — and unpredictably — from person to person.

flashcards.back_html: Large numbers of "foamy" immune cells packed with fat droplets absorbed from damaged myelin — and these cells appear to switch from repairing the brain to fueling ongoing damage and inflammation.

flashcards.prompt: Where does the fat inside these 'foamy' immune cells come from?

choices.text: Myelin, the nerve coating that MS damages
Dietary fat circulating in the bloodstream
Fat cells that migrated from elsewhere in the body

flashcards.explanation_html: The fat droplets come from myelin debris the immune cells absorb while trying to clean up damage — and overloading on it may be what turns them harmful.
